content: This document is an updated version of a Cochrane review that was initially published in 2001 and subsequently updated in 2007 and 2009. Vocal cord nodules are bilateral, benign growths that resemble calluses and are located on the mid-portion of the membranous vocal folds. These nodules vary in size and are histologically characterized by epithelial thickening, often accompanied by varying degrees of inflammation in the underlying superficial lamina propria. Clinically, they are associated with symptoms such as hoarseness, vocal discomfort, and instability of the voice during speaking or singing. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of surgical interventions compared to non-surgical treatments for managing vocal cord nodules. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, BIOSIS Previews, Cambridge Scientific Abstracts, ISRCTN, and other sources for both published and unpublished trials. The most recent search was performed on April 9, 2012. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized or quasi-randomized trials that compared any surgical intervention for vocal cord nodules with non-surgical treatments or no treatment at all. However, no studies meeting these criteria were identified during the search. As a result, the review concluded that there is currently no high-quality evidence available to determine the relative effectiveness of surgical versus non-surgical treatments for vocal cord nodules. The authors emphasized the need for well-designed, high-quality randomized controlled trials to address this gap in evidence.
